html:
The Burke and Wills expedition was a British colonial attempt in 1860 and 1861 to cross Australia from south to north, from Melbourne to the Gulf of Carpentaria. Its leaders reached the tidal waters of the north but died on the way back, and it became Australia's most famous exploring disaster.

Funded by the colony of Victoria and led by the police officer Robert O'Hara Burke, with William Wills as surveyor, it left Melbourne in August 1860 with nineteen men, horses and imported camels. It moved slowly to Menindee on the Darling River, and then to Cooper Creek, where Burke left a depot party.

Burke, Wills, Charles Gray and John King pushed north and in February 1861 reached the mangroves of the Flinders River, among the Mayi-Kulan people, without seeing the open sea. On the way back Gray died. The other three reached the Cooper depot on 21 April, only hours after the depot party had left. Burke and Wills died near there around the end of June. King survived because the Yandruwandha people fed and sheltered him, until a search party found him in September.

The search parties mapped much of the interior, and pastoralists soon moved into the lands of peoples such as the Wangkumara.
